meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Whenever I Feel the Urge to Exercise I Lie Down Until It Goes Away'?
meta.ogDescription: Depew died in 1928. The earliest documented printing, June 1937, credits animator Paul Terry — and names Depew only as a famous hater of exercise.

answer.label: Not Chauncey Depew — first credited to animator Paul Terry
answer.sourceLine: Chauncey Depew died on 5 April 1928. The joke’s earliest documented printing is a New York gossip column of 13 June 1937, which gives the line to Terrytoons animator Paul Terry and mentions Depew only as a byword for hating exercise — not as its author. Depew was credited directly for the first time seven months later, in a newspaper filler of 17 January 1938, nearly ten years after his death.

source.excerpt: GOTHAM GOINGS ON: Paul Terry, who does the animated cartoons, shares Chauncey M. Depew’s contempt for exercise … “When I feel like exercising,” he says, “I just lie down until the feeling goes away.”
trail: The earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator is a syndicated New York gossip column printed on 13 June 1937, which gives the remark to animator Paul Terry and names Depew only as a fellow despiser of exercise (Quote Investigator ↗). Reader’s Digest credited Terry again in January 1938, and the Yale Book of Quotations files the line under his name.

Chauncey Depew died on 5 April 1928 at the age of ninety-three (Wikipedia ↗), so the first item to put the words in his mouth — an untitled filler in Ohio’s Circleville Herald on 17 January 1938 — is posthumous by nearly a decade.

Mark Twain, the other name this joke is pinned on, is tied to it no earlier than an October 1937 speech at Williams College — the earliest Twain connection Quote Investigator located, long after his death in 1910 — and the joke has not been found anywhere in his work. His documented view of exercise, from his seventieth-birthday dinner speech, runs: “Exercise is loathsome” (Project Gutenberg ↗).

Quote Investigator’s verdict is that the preponderance of evidence favours Paul Terry, with Edna May Oliver and Jimmy Durante as rival contenders — and it notes one unchecked lead, a 1936 doctoral thesis that may contain the Durante version and would then be earlier (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The ellipsis is in the original. Note what Depew is doing in this sentence: he is the benchmark for hating exercise, and the line itself belongs to Terry. Quoted from the transcription in Quote Investigator ↗, which cites the page image via GenealogyBank.

source.useLine: The earliest documented printing (13 June 1937) is a columnist’s report of someone else’s remark rather than an authored text, and it falls well after the pre-1931 cutoff for automatic US public domain — so there’s no rights status to give. Credit it as shown above, don’t present it as public domain, and get permission for commercial or published reuse.
source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim can honestly be made for this wording. The version people quote matches no single sourced original — it is a floating newspaper gag, and even its earliest documented printing, on 13 June 1937, is a columnist’s report of someone else’s remark rather than an authored text. That date falls well after the pre-1931 cutoff for automatic US public domain, and the line has never been traced to anything Chauncey Depew published, so the status of the exact wording is undetermined.

author.name: Paul Terry
author.heading: Who actually gets the credit
author.bio: Paul Houlton Terry was an American cartoonist, animator, screenwriter, director and producer who turned out over 1,300 cartoons between 1915 and 1955, and whose Terrytoons studio gave the world Mighty Mouse, Heckle and Jeckle and Gandy Goose. He was famously unsentimental about his own trade — “Walt Disney is the Tiffany’s of the business, and I am the Woolworth’s” — and it is his name, not Depew’s, that sits on the first known printing of the exercise joke in June 1937. Quote Investigator calls him the leading candidate rather than a certainty: the actress Edna May Oliver and the comedian Jimmy Durante were both credited within a year, and the trail may yet run earlier.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been handed this line
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most promiscuously attributed jokes in English. Within roughly fifteen years of its first printing it had been given to an animator, an actress, a comedian, a university president, a humorist, a parodist, a dead senator and a dead novelist — and the modern internet mostly settled on the two dead men.

items.why: Depew died on 5 April 1928 (Wikipedia ↗). The first printing to assign him the words directly is an untitled filler in the Circleville Herald of Ohio on 17 January 1938 — “Chauncey M. Depew… said of exercise, ‘Whenever I feel like it, I just lie down until the feeling goes away’” — seven months after the column that credited Paul Terry (Quote Investigator ↗).

The earliest Twain connection Quote Investigator found is a speech at the induction of the new president of Williams College on 8 October 1937 — twenty-seven years after Twain’s death in 1910 — and the joke has not been found anywhere in his work. What Twain did say about exercise, at his seventieth-birthday dinner in 1905, was blunter and quite different: “Exercise is loathsome” (Project Gutenberg ↗).

In December 1938 the writer J. P. McEvoy profiled the young University of Chicago president in The American Mercury and said Hutchins “holds with that hero who confessed” the exercise joke — crediting an unnamed third party. After that piece the words were regularly ascribed to Hutchins himself, and sometimes to McEvoy (Quote Investigator ↗).

A 1950 shaving-products advertisement in Life credited “the late Bob Benchley”; a 1952 item in the Lethbridge Herald gave it to Max Beerbohm. Neither claim carries any earlier evidence (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented owner of the joke is the animator Paul Terry, in Lucius Beebe’s column of 13 June 1937 — with the actress Edna May Oliver credited two weeks later and Jimmy Durante a year after that, and with Depew appearing in that very first printing only as the standard reference for a man who despised exercise (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the joke landed on Depew
lead: Chauncey Depew is exactly the kind of name jokes migrate to. He ran the New York Central Railroad, sat in the US Senate for twelve years, was one of the most sought-after after-dinner speakers in America, and then did the single most useful thing a wit can do for his posthumous reputation: he lived to ninety-three. Any gag about staying healthy by doing nothing had an obvious peg to hang on.

The first known printing shows the mechanism happening in slow motion. In June 1937 the columnist Lucius Beebe wrote that the animator Paul Terry “shares Chauncey M. Depew’s contempt for exercise” — Depew is the yardstick, Terry is the speaker. Seven months later a filler item had dropped the yardstick and handed Depew the line itself. He had been dead since 1928.
context.detailsSummary: Two loose ends worth knowing about
detailsBody: Quote Investigator flags one unresolved thread: a 1938 philosophy book by John R. Reid quotes the gag as a current Jimmy Durante routine, and that book was a revision of a 1936 Berkeley PhD thesis. If the Durante line was already in the thesis, it would predate the 1937 column — but QI has not seen the thesis, so the 1937 printing stands as the earliest confirmed one.

Depew attracted the other famous exercise joke the same way. Quote Investigator’s separate study of “I get my exercise acting as a pallbearer to my friends who exercise” finds the earliest evidence pointing to the newspaperman William Allen White by 1925, with Depew credited in 1930 — again, after his death — and Mark Twain only in 1950.
context.pull: In the first printing, Depew is the comparison — not the speaker.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Chauncey Depew, who died in 1928 — the words were not assigned to him until January 1938. The earliest documented credit, in a column of 13 June 1937, is to animator Paul Terry, whom Quote Investigator calls the leading candidate rather than a certainty: Edna May Oliver and Jimmy Durante are also contenders, and QI notes that additional evidence may shift the evaluation.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest evidence located by Quote Investigator is a syndicated New York gossip column of 13 June 1937 (Cleveland Plain Dealer, "New York Speaking" by Lucius Beebe, p. 12-C) reading: "GOTHAM GOINGS ON: Paul Terry, who does the animated cartoons, shares Chauncey M. Depew's contempt for exercise … 'When I feel like exercising,' he says, 'I just lie down until the feeling goes away.'"

Quote Investigator states that the first cite did not claim Depew crafted the saying, and that "seven months later on January 17, 1938 the words were assigned directly to Depew" in the Circleville Herald (Ohio): "Chauncey M. Depew … said of exercise, 'Whenever I feel like it, I just lie down until the feeling goes away.'"

Quote Investigator's conclusion: "the preponderance of evidence currently suggests that Paul Terry should receive credit for this remark. Edna Mae Oliver is another contender and so is Jimmy Durante"; the Mark Twain ascription (first found 8 October 1937, Williams College) is late and unfounded; the Hutchins credit derives from J. P. McEvoy's December 1938 American Mercury profile that credited an anonymous "hero"; a 1950 Life advertisement credited Robert Benchley and a 1952 Lethbridge Herald item credited Max Beerbohm; Reader's Digest (January 1938) and the Yale Book of Quotations credit Paul Terry; and a 1938 book by John R. Reid quoting a Durante gag derives from a 1936 thesis QI has not seen.

Quote Investigator's separate study of "I take my only exercise acting as a pallbearer to my friends who exercise" concludes the earliest evidence points to William Allen White by 1925, notes "Chauncey Depew died in 1928" and that a 1930 Iowa newspaper article attributed a version of the jest to him, and that the first Mark Twain citation occurred in 1950.

Chauncey Depew was born 23 April 1834 and died 5 April 1928, aged 93; he was president and then board chairman of the New York Central Railroad, a US Senator from New York (1899–1911), and a noted orator and after-dinner speaker.

Paul Houlton Terry was born 19 February 1887 and died 25 October 1971; he was an American cartoonist, animator, screenwriter, film director and producer who produced over 1,300 cartoons between 1915 and 1955, founded Terrytoons, and whose studio's most famous character is Mighty Mouse; he said "Walt Disney is the Tiffany's of the business, and I am the Woolworth's."

Mark Twain's Seventieth Birthday speech contains: "I have never taken any exercise, except sleeping and resting, and I never intend to take any. Exercise is loathsome." — and does not contain the lie-down-until-the-feeling-passes joke.
Edna May Oliver (9 November 1883 – 9 November 1942) was an American stage and film actress.
